body:
Saguna and Nirguna Bhakti

Medieval Bhakti literature developed through different understandings of the divine. Two broad categories are useful for distinguishing its principal literary and religious traditions.

  • Saguna Bhakti: Devotion to God understood as possessing attributes or a recognisable form. Traditions centred on Rama, Krishna, Vishnu and Shiva commonly fall within this category.
  • Nirguna Bhakti: Devotion to a divine reality understood as formless and beyond ordinary physical attributes.

These categories describe different devotional approaches. Individual saints and traditions may use varied philosophical expressions that do not always fit neatly into a single classification.

Nirguna saints and the Sant tradition

Kabir

Kabir, traditionally associated with a weaving community in northern India, is a major representative of Nirguna Bhakti. His compositions criticise religious hypocrisy, caste discrimination and the belief that external ritual alone can produce spiritual liberation.

His poetry uses familiar images, direct expressions and language drawn from regional speech forms. Important forms associated with Kabir include the Sakhi, often a concise instructive couplet, and the Pad, a lyrical devotional composition.

The Bijak is an important collection preserved within the Kabir Panth. Compositions attributed to Kabir are also found in the Kabir Granthavali and the Guru Granth Sahib. Many were collected after his lifetime, and the surviving traditions contain variations.

Guru Nanak and Sikh literary traditions

Guru Nanak lived from 1469 to 1539. His teachings emphasised devotion to the formless divine, honest living, remembrance of God and human equality. His compositions circulated through hymns known as Shabads.

Guru Angad played an important role in the development and standardisation of the Gurmukhi script. In 1604, Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth, incorporating compositions of Sikh Gurus and selected saints from other religious and social backgrounds.

The Sikh scriptural tradition also preserves compositions attributed to Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and Baba Farid. Guru Gobind Singh subsequently declared the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru of the Sikhs.

The Guru Granth Sahib is written in the Gurmukhi script but contains compositions using several linguistic forms. Script and language must therefore be distinguished.

Other Nirguna saints

Ravidas emphasised devotion and spiritual equality, while Dadu Dayal criticised religious divisions and external formalism. Their compositions contributed to the broad North Indian Sant tradition.

Rama and Krishna devotional literature

AuthorImportant work or formLiterary association
TulsidasRamcharitmanasRama devotion in Awadhi
SurdasSursagarKrishna devotion in Braj Bhasha
MirabaiDevotional Padas and BhajansPersonal devotion to Krishna
JayadevaGita GovindaKrishna and Radha devotion in Sanskrit
VidyapatiDevotional and lyrical poetryMaithili literary tradition

Tulsidas composed Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi, making the story of Rama accessible through a major regional literary language. Surdas is traditionally associated with Sursagar, which celebrates Krishna, especially narratives of his childhood and devotional relationships.

Mirabai, associated with Rajasthan and Mewar, composed devotional lyrics expressing intense personal attachment to Krishna. Her compositions circulated across Rajasthan, Gujarat and other regions, developing multiple linguistic versions.

Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, composed in the 12th century in Sanskrit, is an important example of the continued vitality of classical-language devotional literature during the medieval period. Not all Bhakti literature was composed in vernacular languages.

Bhakti literature of eastern India

Bengal

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, active during the late 15th and early 16th centuries, became an influential figure in Krishna devotion in Bengal and Odisha. His movement encouraged collective religious expression and inspired extensive Vaishnava literature.

Important biographical works include Chaitanya Bhagavata by Vrindavana Dasa and Chaitanya Charitamrita by Krishnadasa Kaviraja. These compositions preserve information about the saint and the development of his devotional community.

Early Bengali literature also includes Mangalakavyas, narrative poems celebrating local deities, as well as regional adaptations of the Sanskrit epics.

Assam

Shankardev, also spelled Sankaradeva, developed a major Vaishnava tradition in Assam. His literary contributions include devotional songs known as Borgeets, religious plays called Ankiya Nats and compositions such as Kirtana Ghosha.

Institutions such as Namghars, or congregational prayer halls, and Satras, religious institutions associated with the tradition, helped preserve and transmit devotional literature.

Social significance

Bhakti poetry widened participation in literary and religious expression. Artisans, women, cultivators and people from diverse caste backgrounds contributed to devotional traditions. Nevertheless, the social positions and teachings of individual movements varied, and not every Bhakti tradition rejected existing social institutions in the same way.

Prelims focus

  • Kabir is a major Nirguna saint and is associated with the Bijak.
  • Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.
  • Ramcharitmanas is in Awadhi; Sursagar is associated with Braj Bhasha.
  • Jayadeva composed Gita Govinda in Sanskrit.
  • Shankardev is associated with Assamese Vaishnava literature, Borgeets and Ankiya Nats.
  • Trap: Gurmukhi is a script, not the only language represented in the Guru Granth Sahib.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapters 8 and 9, pp. 112–119 and 130–134; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, pp. 142–144 and 161–166; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapter 7, pp. 36–40, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Nirguna links the formless divine with Kabir and Guru Nanak; Saguna links Rama with Tulsidas and Krishna with Surdas and Mirabai.
pictures.caption: Saguna and Nirguna devotional traditions

title: Northern and Eastern Indian Bhakti Literature

body:
Sufism and literary expression

Sufism refers to mystical traditions within Islam that emphasise spiritual purification, devotion, divine love and the relationship between a seeker and God. Sufi literature expresses these ideas through poetry, conversations, letters, biographies and instructional works.

In medieval India, Sufi authors used Persian, Hindavi, Punjabi, Dakhini and several other regional languages. Their choice of language depended on their audience, literary tradition and purpose.

Institutions that supported Sufi literary culture

  • Silsila: A spiritual lineage or order connecting teachers and disciples.
  • Pir or Shaikh: A spiritual guide or teacher.
  • Murid: A disciple who follows a spiritual teacher.
  • Khanqah: A hospice or institutional centre where a Sufi teacher and disciples gathered.
  • Dargah: A shrine associated with the tomb of a Sufi saint.

Khanqahs provided opportunities for teaching, discussion, hospitality and the communication of religious ideas. The teachings of influential saints were frequently remembered and recorded by their disciples.

Principal forms of Sufi literature

Literary formMeaning or function
MalfuzatRecorded conversations and discourses of Sufi saints
MaktubatCollections of letters written by spiritual teachers
TazkiraBiographical accounts of saints and religious figures
MasnaviExtended narrative poem, often presenting spiritual or romantic themes
GhazalLyric poetic form used to express love and related themes, including mystical devotion
PremakhyanNarrative of love that may symbolise the spiritual search for the divine

Major authors and works

Al-Hujwiri

Ali bin Usman al-Hujwiri, associated with Lahore, composed the Kashf-ul-Mahjub in Persian during the 11th century. The work explains Sufi teachings, practices and traditions.

Amir Khusrau

Amir Khusrau lived from 1253 to 1325. He was a poet associated with the courts of the Delhi Sultanate and a disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya.

He composed major works in Persian and is also remembered for compositions associated with Hindavi. His literary activities illustrate the interaction between Persian courtly culture and Indian regional expression.

Important Persian works associated with him include Khazain-ul-Futuh and Nuh Sipihr. Khazain-ul-Futuh is associated with the reign of Alauddin Khalji, while Nuh Sipihr contains descriptions praising aspects of India and its cultural life.

Amir Hasan Sijzi

Amir Hasan Sijzi compiled the Fawaid-ul-Fuad, a collection of the conversations of Nizamuddin Auliya. It is a major example of Malfuzat literature.

Do not confuse the 2 authors

Amir Khusrau and Amir Hasan Sijzi were both associated with Nizamuddin Auliya. However, Fawaid-ul-Fuad was compiled by Amir Hasan Sijzi, not Amir Khusrau.

Baba Farid

Fariduddin Ganjshakar, commonly known as Baba Farid, is associated with the Chishti order and early Punjabi devotional poetry. Compositions attributed to him are preserved in the Guru Granth Sahib, illustrating the circulation of religious literature across community boundaries.

Malik Muhammad Jayasi

Malik Muhammad Jayasi composed Padmavat in Awadhi in the 16th century. It belongs to the tradition of Sufi romantic narratives.

The story of Ratansen, Padmavati and Chittor incorporates the theme of human love as a means of expressing the spiritual quest. As a literary romance, it should not be treated as a contemporary historical account of the earlier Khalji conquest of Chittor.

Major Sufi orders and regional centres

Order or traditionImportant figureAssociated centre
ChishtiMuinuddin ChishtiAjmer
ChishtiNizamuddin AuliyaDelhi
ChishtiBaba FaridAjodhan, now Pakpattan
SuhrawardiBahauddin ZakariyaMultan
ChishtiGesu DarazGulbarga, now Kalaburagi

The Deccan became an important region of interaction between Sufi teachings and regional languages, including Dakhini. In Gujarat, Sufi centres and devotional traditions also contributed to a multilingual religious culture.

Ginans and Gujarat's religious literary heritage

Ginans are devotional and instructional compositions associated particularly with the Khoja Nizari Ismaili tradition. Their languages include Gujarati, Kachchi, Sindhi, Punjabi and other regional forms.

The Ginans demonstrate how religious ideas originating within Islamic traditions could be expressed through Indian literary and linguistic conventions. They represent a related but distinct tradition and should not be classified automatically as the literature of a particular Sufi order.

Bhakti and Sufi literary interaction

Bhakti and Sufi traditions shared certain features, including the use of regional languages, oral transmission, devotional poetry and emphasis on an individual's relationship with the divine.

However, they emerged from distinct religious traditions. Similarity in poetic themes does not mean that their theological beliefs and institutional practices were identical.

Prelims focus

  • Malfuzat records conversations; Maktubat contains letters; Tazkira contains biographies.
  • Amir Khusrau was a disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya.
  • Amir Hasan Sijzi compiled Fawaid-ul-Fuad.
  • Jayasi composed Padmavat in Awadhi.
  • Baba Farid's compositions occur in the Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Trap: Khanqah refers to a Sufi institutional centre, while Dargah refers to a saint's tomb-shrine.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapter 8, pp. 110–115; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Theme 6, pp. 151–159 and 161–166; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standard 7, 2021–22, Chapter 7, pp. 36–40, consulted online 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Sufi communities recorded conversations as Malfuzat, collected letters as Maktubat, preserved saints’ lives as Tazkira, and shared ideas through poetry and regional languages.
pictures.caption: Formation of Sufi literary traditions

title: Sufi Literature and Indo-Persian Cultural Interaction

body:
Literature under medieval patronage

Medieval rulers supported poets, historians, scholars and translators to record dynastic history, celebrate political achievements, express cultural ideals and develop the prestige of their courts.

Courtly literature was composed in Sanskrit, Persian and various regional languages. Royal support enabled authors to produce extensive works, while manuscript workshops and religious institutions helped preserve them.

Heroic and bardic traditions

Heroic literature developed around narratives of courage, loyalty, honour, political authority and the achievements of rulers and warriors. In western and northern India, Charans, Bhats and other bardic communities preserved genealogies, poems and stories through oral recitation and written compositions.

The Raso tradition is particularly associated with heroic narrative literature in Rajasthan and adjoining regions. Its compositions often combine historical memories with legend and poetic elaboration.

WorkTraditional authorPrincipal association
Prithviraj RasoChand BardaiPrithviraj Chauhan
Visaldeva RasoNarapati NalhaRajput courtly and heroic traditions
Alha KhandTraditionally associated with JagnikAlha and Udal of Bundelkhand
Kanhadade PrabandhaPadmanabhaKanhadade of Jalore

The Prithviraj Raso is traditionally attributed to Chand Bardai, but its surviving versions contain material added over time. It is valuable for studying heroic traditions and later memories of Prithviraj Chauhan, but not every episode can be accepted as a contemporary historical fact.

Padmanabha's Kanhadade Prabandha, composed in the 15th century, is important to the literary heritage of Gujarat and Rajasthan. It illustrates how historical events could be remembered and reshaped in regional narrative literature.

Persian chronicles of the Delhi Sultanate

Persian chroniclers recorded the activities of medieval rulers, political events, administrative institutions and court life.

AuthorWorkAssociation
Minhaj-us-SirajTabaqat-i-NasiriEarly Delhi Sultanate
Ziauddin BaraniTarikh-i-Firuz ShahiPolitical history of the Delhi Sultanate
Ziauddin BaraniFatwa-i-JahandariPolitical and governing ideals
Shams-i-Siraj AfifTarikh-i-Firuz ShahiReign of Firuz Shah Tughlaq
Amir KhusrauKhazain-ul-FutuhAchievements of Alauddin Khalji

Barani's historical chronicle and his work on political ideals serve different purposes. The similar title Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi is also associated with Shams-i-Siraj Afif, whose work concentrates on Firuz Shah Tughlaq's reign.

Mughal literature and historical chronicles

The Mughal court promoted Persian as a major language of administration, intellectual life and historical writing. Important chronicles and memoirs provide extensive information about the empire.

WorkAuthorPrincipal subject
BaburnamaBaburAutobiographical account of his life and campaigns
HumayunnamaGulbadan BegumHumayun and the Mughal royal household
AkbarnamaAbu'l FazlHistory and reign of Akbar
Ain-i-AkbariAbu'l FazlAdministration, economy and society under Akbar
Tuzuk-i-JahangiriJahangirImperial memoirs
PadshahnamaAbdul Hamid LahoriHistory of the reign of Shah Jahan

The Baburnama was originally composed in Chagatai Turkish. A Persian translation was prepared during Akbar's reign. The original language of the work must therefore be distinguished from the language through which it later circulated widely at the Mughal court.

The Akbarnama consists of 3 books. Its 3rd book, the Ain-i-Akbari, presents systematic information about the imperial administration, military arrangements, revenue system, economy and society.

Gulbadan Begum's Humayunnama is particularly valuable because it provides perspectives on the royal household, family relationships and the experiences of royal women.

Translations and manuscript production

Akbar supported the translation of several Sanskrit works into Persian. The Persian adaptation of the Mahabharata became known as the Razmnama, meaning the Book of War. The Ramayana was also translated into Persian under Mughal patronage.

Imperial manuscript workshops, known as Kitabkhanas, brought together calligraphers, painters, scholars and other specialists. Their activities contributed to the preservation of literary works and the development of illustrated manuscripts.

Literature under the Vijayanagara rulers

The Vijayanagara Empire supported literary activities in Sanskrit, Telugu, Kannada and Tamil. Krishnadevaraya, who ruled from 1509 to 1529, was both a ruler and an important literary patron.

He composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu, a devotional poetic work connected with Andal and Vishnu devotion. His court is also associated with eminent Telugu poets traditionally remembered as the Ashtadiggajas.

Allasani Peddana, one of these poets, is associated with Manucharitramu. Vijayanagara patronage illustrates how regional languages could attain high literary prestige alongside Sanskrit.

Historical value and limitations

Royal chronicles, heroic poetry and courtly biographies are important sources for reconstructing political history, institutions, cultural ideals and social life. However, authors depended on their patrons and wrote with particular political or literary purposes.

Historical reconstruction therefore requires comparison between literary narratives, inscriptions, administrative records and other evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Prithviraj Raso is traditionally attributed to Chand Bardai.
  • Baburnama was originally composed in Chagatai Turkish.
  • Gulbadan Begum wrote Humayunnama.
  • Ain-i-Akbari forms the 3rd book of Abu'l Fazl's Akbarnama.
  • Razmnama is the Persian adaptation of the Mahabharata.
  • Krishnadevaraya composed Amuktamalyada in Telugu.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts II, Class 7, 2020–21, Chapters 3, 4 and 9, particularly pp. 124–126; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Class 12, Themes 7 and 9, pp. 170–193, 226–231 and 242–243; Gujarat State School Textbook Board, Social Science, Standards 7 and 10, chapters on regional culture and literary heritage; Gujarati Vishwakosh, Kanhadade Prabandha entry, consulted online 26 November 2026.]
